analysis.title: AI in 2027: 20 questions for the global economy
key_insights: Base case is a plateau, not a bust: AI investment keeps rising in 2027, supported by strong demand and constrained supply, but its contribution to US growth is probably close to its peak because GDP responds to the change in investment, not its level.

US investment in data centre structures, computers and software reached 5.6% of GDP in Q2 2026, up from 3.8% in 2022 (5.2% net of imported hardware). That is above the dotcom peak of about 4.5% but below Britain's 1840s railway mania at roughly 6-7%.

AI-related investment accounts for 37% of US real GDP growth, versus 16-18% for IT investment in 1998-2000. Outside AI, the rest of US private non-residential investment fell year-on-year for six consecutive quarters by mid-2026, so the boom appears to redirect investment rather than add to it.

Financing is shifting from hyperscaler cash flows toward debt, private credit and off-balance-sheet structures (SPVs, leases, GPU-backed loans, ABS/CMBS). Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Oracle have issued jumbo bonds since 2025, with Oracle the most leveraged. Several big tech firms announced equity raises in June.

Neoclouds and AI labs depend on outside money (venture capital, private credit, vendor financing) and are the most likely point of stress if financing tightens. Cash-rich hyperscalers can absorb a disappointment in AI returns.

Second wave of investment in grids, power generation and cooling is slower and longer-lived than the chip build-out. Rule of thumb of US$1bn per 25MW implies more than 12GW of added power demand if half of the c.US$1tn 2027 hyperscaler capex goes to AI compute. Rising power bills are becoming a political issue and feed into inflation.
GPUs may have an economic life of three to six years, versus decades for rails, fibre, grids and substations. That shorter shelf life is central to the debate over returns.

AI is inflationary near term (energy demand, memory chip prices, electricians, transformers, construction) and probably disinflationary later, mostly in services. The ING view is that the disinflation dividend is a second-half-of-the-decade story, not a 2027 story.

Europe is far behind on AI investment (US imports of computer equipment and semiconductors up about 258% since 2019 versus 38% in the UK) but supplies critical inputs: ASML expects EUR44-45bn of 2026 sales and Infineon expects AI revenues to rise from about EUR1.5bn in FY2026 to EUR2.5bn in FY2027. Europe is less exposed to a bust, with equities at 13% of UK household financial assets versus 44% in the US.

Labour market effect so far is on hiring, not layoffs. Stanford Digital Economy Lab data show employment among 22-25-year-olds in highly exposed occupations about 19% below trend by June 2026. A soft payrolls print could signal either weakness or higher productivity, which complicates central bank reads.

Productivity: US labour productivity has picked up, partly from capital-heavy data centre investment, while total factor productivity has improved without an exceptional acceleration. China's labour productivity growth has picked up over the last two years. ING expects a J-curve with possibly abrupt gains later.

Vendor financing and circular deals (chipmakers taking stakes in AI labs and neoclouds that buy their chips) inflate reported demand and create concentration risk. ING says this is not Lucent/Nortel again because balance sheets are far stronger and US corporate debt-to-GDP is not worrisome.

Monetary policy is unlikely to be the trigger for a bust, but an energy shock keeps inflation above target, so central banks have less room to cut than in 2001. Long-end yields and term premia matter more than the policy rate for debt-funded AI investment. Some form of government support in a bust is conceivable.

ING forecasts total hyperscaler bond issuance of around US$280bn in 2027 (about US$190bn in USD and US$65bn in EUR/EUR60bn) and net TMT supply of EUR103bn in European credit, including US$65bn from hyperscalers.

Valuations: Microsoft P/E expected to fall from 29.2x (FY2026 earnings) to 21.9x in 2028, Amazon from 28x to 21x in 2027, Alphabet from 20.9x to 17.9x. Leaders are profitable, so ING sees bubble-like pockets, not a bubble across the board. The largest tech stocks' weight in the S&P 500 exceeds the dotcom peak.

Revenue gap: Amazon, Microsoft and Alphabet invested around US$600bn over 2023-25. At 40-50 cents of annual revenue per dollar of AI infrastructure, ING estimates US$240-300bn a year of revenue is needed, though not all capex was AI-related.

Biggest risk to the boom is overcapacity from chip and model efficiency gains, a slow squeeze through eroding margins and tighter financing rather than a single trigger. Cheaper models are an intriguing risk (DeepSeek in January 2025 wiped almost US$600bn off Nvidia's market value in one day), and Nvidia's margins could normalise.

A 30% equity correction would cut about $24.5tn of household wealth, implying a consumer spending drop of roughly $640bn (2.9% of nominal consumer spending) at a 2.6 cent marginal propensity to consume, or about 2.4% at 2.2 cents. The larger damage would come through business investment and jobs, as after the dotcom bust when business investment fell 11% in two years.

An AI-led tech sell-off could hurt the dollar rather than lift it, through foreign repatriation and higher hedge ratios, with the IMF estimating a dollar fall of about 6%. Yen and Swiss franc would act as safe havens, the euro could benefit relatively, and the Taiwan dollar and Korean won would be pressured.

Signposts: hyperscaler capex guidance, Taiwanese order books and lead times, AI revenues relative to capex, credit spreads on AI-related debt, private credit flows and redemptions, bond yields and term premia, non-tech investment, hiring in AI-exposed sectors, and grid and power data.

Taiwan's leading semiconductor companies report order books full on a rolling 18-month basis, and industry forecasts point to tight supply-demand conditions until 2028. Hyperscaler capex is expected to exceed US$1 trillion in 2027.

sector_views.rationale: Clearest winners of the build-out, already seeing it in order books, with tight supply expected until 2028.

sector_views.sector: Utilities, grid operators and electrical equipment
sector_views.rationale: Second wave of investment in transmission, generation, cooling and construction has longer-lived assets and is less vulnerable to a sudden AI downturn.
AI is a selling point but threatens per-seat pricing if one employee with an agent does the work of five.

sector_views.sector: Legacy IT services, BPO, call centres, search-dependent media and advertising
sector_views.rationale: Business models are the very tasks AI now performs, so most at risk of disruption.
AI assistants increasingly do the browsing and booking.
Listed among the suppliers of the build-out seeing strength in order books.

earnings_insights: ASML expects EUR44-45bn of sales in 2026 and says customers keep raising their equipment-demand forecasts (company guidance, not a reported actual).
Infineon expects AI-related revenues to rise from around EUR1.5bn in FY2026 to EUR2.5bn in FY2027 (company expectation).

Microsoft P/E is expected to fall from 29.2x on fiscal 2026 earnings to 21.9x in 2028, Amazon from 28x on 2025 earnings to 21x in 2027, and Alphabet from 20.9x to 17.9x over the same period (analyst expectations). Earnings estimates are higher than a couple of months ago.
Capex is absorbing a rising share of hyperscaler operating cash flow, squeezing free cash flow and leaving less room for share buybacks.

macro_indicators.indicator: AI-related investment share of US real GDP growth
macro_indicators.interpretation: ING estimate net of imports, versus 16-18% for IT investment in 1998-2000. Contribution likely peaks in 2027.

macro_indicators.indicator: US data centre structures, computers and software investment, share of GDP
macro_indicators.interpretation: Above the 2000 dotcom peak of about 4.5%, below the 1840s UK railway mania of roughly 6-7%.
Another year of heavy AI investment expected, constrained by supply of chips, power, permits and electricians.
ING forecast of rising debt funding, with net European TMT supply of EUR103bn.

macro_indicators.reading: Down year-on-year for six consecutive quarters
macro_indicators.interpretation: AI boom appears to redirect rather than add investment.
Same as 2001 and well below the 100% of 2007, so a tech sell-off is not a 2008-style household balance sheet shock.
Base for the estimated 2.4-2.9% hit from a 30% equity correction.

risk_factors: Overcapacity from chip, model and algorithm efficiency gains pushing down utilisation and returns.

Financing stress: rising bond yields and term premia, a credit event at a leveraged neocloud or private credit fund, or redemption gates at semi-liquid private credit vehicles sold to retail and wealth clients.
Disappointing enterprise demand if pilots fail to turn into profits.
Cheaper-model breakthrough lowering AI lab margins and normalising Nvidia's margins.
Circular financing and concentration risk among the same handful of firms acting as investors, suppliers, landlords and tenants.
Energy shock keeping central banks hawkish, with less room to cut than in 2001 and limited fiscal space.
Power bottlenecks and rising electricity bills creating political pushback.
Taiwan crisis or escalation of export controls hitting the countries most dependent on the AI supply chain.
Capex guidance revisions downward if announced capacity commitments, possibly strategic entry deterrence, are not fully executed.
vol_and_positioning: Weight of the largest tech stocks in the S&P 500 exceeds the dotcom peak, so any disappointment would hit the whole index hard.
Foreign investors hold large, partly unhedged positions in US equities, so a US tech sell-off could trigger repatriation and higher hedge ratios, which are dollar-negative.
Top 20% of US households by income hold 84.1% of equities, mutual funds and defined-contribution assets, limiting the wealth effect of a sell-off.
geopolitical: Export controls on advanced chips to China, tariffs and subsidy programmes such as the US Chips Act are pushing companies to build capacity closer to home or in friendly countries, making the chain more resilient but more expensive.
A Taiwan crisis is described as a low-probability, extreme-impact risk to the AI supply chain.
An energy shock is keeping inflation above target in the US and Europe.
Government support for strategically important AI companies is conceivable in a bust, including public procurement and guarantees.
Data centre moratoria in Dublin and Amsterdam and the EU AI gigafactories initiative reflect Europe's constraints on energy and grid capacity.

tension_points.bull_case: Order books at Taiwan's leading chipmakers are full on a rolling 18-month basis and supply is tight until 2028, so hyperscaler capex above US$1tn in 2027 is likely. Leaders are profitable and much less leveraged than dotcom-era firms.
tension_points.bear_case: Capex is running ahead of AI revenues, with US$240-300bn a year of revenue needed. Financing is shifting to debt, private credit and opaque structures, and overcapacity could produce a slow squeeze of margins and returns.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Shortening lead times for chips and equipment, cancelled or postponed data centre projects, capex guidance that stops being revised up, and a widening gap between investment and AI revenues.

tension_points.bull_case: Hyperscalers are investment-grade with strong balance sheets, many vendor contracts look like normal commercial arrangements, and US corporate debt-to-GDP is not worrisome.
tension_points.bear_case: Circular deals inflate reported demand and create concentration risk, with neoclouds and AI labs reliant on outside money and private credit exposed through semi-liquid retail vehicles.
tension_points.what_invalidates: The trail of money getting longer before it reaches a customer who is not also an investor, plus credit events at a leveraged neocloud or private credit fund.

tension_points.bull_case: Higher productivity should lower unit labour costs and exert disinflationary pressure, mostly in services.
tension_points.bear_case: Near term, AI demand for energy, memory chips, labour and construction adds to inflation, and dynamic pricing could make prices stickier.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Productivity gains showing up in the statistics, which ING expects in the second half of the decade rather than in 2027.

theme_stances.key_argument: Financing is moving from hyperscaler cash flows to debt, private credit and off-balance-sheet structures, raising risk if returns fail to appear.
theme_stances.evidence: It is gradually turning into a credit story.

theme_stances.key_argument: An AI-led correction would be a US-centric shock that could trigger repatriation and hurt the dollar rather than lift it.
theme_stances.evidence: in an AI bust, the dollar may lose its reputation as the place to hide.
